```{python}
from __future__ import annotations

import sys
from pathlib import Path

import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
import pyfixest as pf
from matplotlib.colors import BoundaryNorm, ListedColormap

import pypanelsim as pps

TREATMENT_CMAP = ListedColormap(["#f7f7f7", "#252525"])
TREATMENT_NORM = BoundaryNorm([-0.5, 0.5, 1.5], TREATMENT_CMAP.N)

VIGNETTE = Path.cwd()
ROOT = VIGNETTE.parents[1]
sys.path.insert(0, str(ROOT))

from examples.baker_twfe import (  # noqa: E402
    baker_frame,
    fit_baker_event_studies,
    plot_baker_event_studies,
)
```

## The failure design

[Baker, Larcker, and Wang's JFE replication](https://github.com/andrewchbaker/JFE_DID)
contains a deliberately simple staggered-adoption design in
`Code/1g. Failures With Event Studies and Heterogeneity.R`. Fifty state
clusters are randomly divided into three adoption cohorts: 17 states adopt in
1989, 18 in 1998, and 15 in 2007. Cohort effects are positive and grow linearly
after adoption, but their slopes decline from 0.10 to 0.05 to 0.01.

For unit $i$ in cohort $G_i=g$, `pypanelsim` implements

$$
Y_{it} = \alpha_i + \gamma_t + \varepsilon_{it}
       + W_{it}s_g(t-g+1),
\qquad
W_{it}=\mathbb{1}\{t\geq g\}.
$$

There are no anticipation effects and no structural pre-trends. Yet a vanilla
relative-time TWFE regression combines valid not-yet-treated comparisons with
comparisons that use already-treated units as controls. Because treatment
effects differ across cohorts and event time, those comparisons contaminate
one another.

The original code samples unit effects, time effects, and residuals from a
private Compustat panel. The self-contained implementation uses centered
Gaussian additive effects and errors instead. It preserves the part of the DGP
that causes the failure: the calendar, randomized state cohorts, treatment
timing, and dynamic cohort heterogeneity.

```{python}
SEED = 28101695
config = pps.BakerPanelConfig()
panel = pps.baker(config=config, seed=SEED)

pd.DataFrame(
    {
        "adoption year": config.adoption_years,
        "states": config.cohort_state_counts,
        "units in this draw": [
            np.sum(panel.adoption_times == period)
            for period in config.adoption_periods
        ],
        "effect slope": config.cohort_effect_slopes,
    }
)
```

The default draw has 1,000 units over 1980--2015. Assignment is randomized at
the state level, so every unit within a state adopts together.

```{python}
#| label: fig-baker-matrices
#| fig-cap: "One Baker draw. Rows are units ordered by randomized state cohort; columns are calendar years."
#| fig-width: 13
#| fig-height: 5

order = np.argsort(panel.adoption_times, kind="stable")
figure, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(13, 5), constrained_layout=True)

outcome_image = axes[0].matshow(panel.outcome[order], aspect="auto", cmap="viridis")
axes[0].set_title("Observed outcome Y")
axes[0].set_xlabel("Calendar year")
axes[0].set_ylabel("Units ordered by adoption cohort")
figure.colorbar(outcome_image, ax=axes[0], fraction=0.03)

treatment_image = axes[1].matshow(
    panel.treatment[order],
    aspect="auto",
    cmap=TREATMENT_CMAP,
    norm=TREATMENT_NORM,
)
axes[1].set_title("Treatment W")
axes[1].set_xlabel("Calendar year")
treatment_bar = figure.colorbar(
    treatment_image,
    ax=axes[1],
    fraction=0.03,
    ticks=(0, 1),
)
treatment_bar.ax.set_yticklabels(["Untreated", "Treated"])

ticks = np.arange(0, config.n_periods, 5)
for axis in axes:
    axis.set_xticks(ticks, config.years[ticks])

plt.show()
```

## Vanilla relative-time TWFE

We bin all leads before $-6$ and lags after $6$, omit event time $-1$, and fit
unit and period fixed effects with state-clustered standard errors. The
executable PyFixest call is:

```{python}
frame = baker_frame(panel, config)
window = 5
frame["event_time_binned"] = frame["rel_time"].clip(
    lower=-(window + 1), upper=window + 1
)

twfe_fit = pf.feols(
    "outcome ~ i(event_time_binned, ref=-1) | unit + time",
    frame,
    vcov={"CRV1": "state"},
)
```

This is the conventional event-study regression, not a cohort-specific design.
The [PyFixest difference-in-differences guide](https://pyfixest.org/difference-in-differences.html)
uses the same `i(relative_time, ref=-1) | unit + year` construction for a
vanilla TWFE event study.

## Saturated cohort-by-event-time estimator

The correction fully interacts treatment cohort with event time, then
aggregates the cohort-specific estimates using cohort shares. This is the
saturated Sun--Abraham-style estimator exposed by PyFixest:

```{python}
last_cohort = config.adoption_periods[-1]
saturated_frame = frame.loc[
    (frame["time"] < last_cohort)
    & ((frame["treatment"] == 0.0) | (frame["rel_time"] <= window))
].copy()
saturated_frame["cohort_for_estimator"] = saturated_frame["cohort_period"].mask(
    saturated_frame["cohort_period"] == last_cohort, 0
)

saturated_fit = pf.event_study(
    saturated_frame,
    yname="outcome",
    idname="unit",
    tname="time",
    gname="cohort_for_estimator",
    estimator="saturated",
    att=False,
    cluster="state",
)
saturated_fit.aggregate(agg="period", weighting="shares").head()
```

All units eventually adopt in the original design. Following the comparison
sample used in the Baker replication, we stop before the 2007 cohort adopts.
That cohort is consequently not yet treated throughout this estimation sample
and is encoded as `g=0`, PyFixest's convention for control units. Treated
cohort observations are retained through event time 5. This prevents
already-treated cohorts from supplying the comparison outcome.

PyFixest documents `estimator="saturated"` as a fully interacted cohort/event-
time specification and provides `aggregate(weighting="shares")` for the
event-time averages; see the
[`SaturatedEventStudy` API](https://pyfixest.org/reference/did.saturated_twfe.SaturatedEventStudy.html).

## Estimates versus known truth

```{python}
#| label: fig-baker-event-study
#| fig-cap: "Vanilla TWFE is contaminated by dynamic cohort heterogeneity; the saturated event study follows its cohort-weighted estimand."
#| fig-width: 13
#| fig-height: 5

estimates = fit_baker_event_studies(panel, config, window=window)
figure, _ = plot_baker_event_studies(estimates)
plt.show()
```

The dashed line is computed directly from `panel.treatment_effect`, not from a
regression. The two panels have different cohort-weighted truths because the
saturated comparison intentionally excludes the final cohort after truncating
the sample.

```{python}
def post_rmse(results):
    post = results.loc[results["event_time"] >= 0]
    return float(np.sqrt(np.mean((post["estimate"] - post["truth"]) ** 2)))

comparison = pd.DataFrame(
    {
        "estimator": ["Vanilla TWFE", "Saturated cohort × event time"],
        "post-period RMSE": [
            post_rmse(estimates["twfe"]),
            post_rmse(estimates["saturated"]),
        ],
    }
)
comparison
```

In this seeded draw, the vanilla estimates eventually become negative even
though all true effects are positive. Its apparent lead coefficients are also
sampling and contamination artifacts: the DGP's pre-treatment effects are
exactly zero. The saturated estimates remain close to the increasing true
effect path because they form cohort-appropriate comparisons before
aggregation.

## Reproduce outside the vignette

The standalone script uses the same seed and writes the comparison figure:

```bash
uv run python examples/baker_twfe.py
```

For a reusable simulator or a different noise scale:

```{python}
noiseless = pps.BakerPanelConfig(n_units=200, noise_scale=0.0)
simulator = pps.baker_design(noiseless)
another_panel = simulator.simulate(seed=7)

another_panel.shape, another_panel.is_absorbing
```
